cards.front: Adrian and Zotterman recorded one stretch receptor ending in a frog muscle under three increasing weights. What did a heavier load change, and what happened while a load was held?
cards.back: Impulses came more often but stayed the same height (rate coding). While a load was held, the frequency slowly fell (adaptation).
cards.quote: They come more often, and they do not get bigger.

cards.front: In a {{c1::labelled line}}, a fibre's activity means one thing, say "sweet", however it was activated.
cards.quote: In a labelled line, a fibre's activity means one thing, say "sweet", however it was activated.

cards.front: Why is pressure on the closed eye seen as light?
cards.back: Activity in the optic nerve means light to the brain, whatever started it. This labelled-line idea is behind Müller's law of specific nerve energies.
cards.quote: The pressure is not light, but activity in the optic nerve means light to the brain, whatever started it.

cards.front: Name two ways stimulus intensity is carried by sensory afferents.
cards.back: The firing frequency of each fibre, and the number of active fibres (a stronger stimulus recruits more afferents).
cards.quote: A stronger stimulus also recruits more afferents, so the number of active fibres carries intensity too.

cards.front: What does a neuron's tuning curve plot?
cards.back: Its mean firing rate against one property of the stimulus, such as the orientation of a bar or the frequency of a tone.
cards.quote: A neuron's tuning curve plots its mean firing rate against one property of the stimulus

cards.front: When the same stimulus is presented many times, the {{c1::standard deviation}} of the trial-to-trial fluctuation in spike count is the neuron's noise.
cards.quote: The standard deviation of that fluctuation is the neuron's noise.

cards.front: In a rate code, what is a sensory neuron's firing rate on any one trial?
cards.back: Its tuning curve read at the stimulus, plus a fluctuation that averages to zero: rate = tuning curve(stimulus) + fluctuation.
cards.why: A spike means nothing by itself; it means what its neuron is tuned to.
cards.quote: on each trial its firing rate is its tuning curve read at the stimulus, plus a fluctuation that averages to zero

cards.front: {{c1::Transduction}} is the conversion of a stimulus into an electrical signal at a sensory receptor.
cards.quote: Transduction is the conversion of a stimulus into an electrical signal at a sensory receptor.

cards.front: The first signal is the {{c1::receptor potential}}, a change in membrane voltage whose size grows with stimulus strength.
cards.quote: The first signal is the receptor potential, a change in membrane voltage whose size grows with stimulus strength.

cards.front: The channel Piezo2 was removed from the sensory neurons and Merkel cells of adult mice, and much of touch was lost. What does this show, and what does it not show?
cards.back: Piezo2 is needed for much of normal touch in mice. It does not show that Piezo2 carries all of touch (much, not all was lost), and it says nothing about senses that were not tested.
cards.quote: Removing the channel Piezo2 from adult mouse sensory neurons and Merkel cells removed much of touch

cards.front: In a passive receptor model (resting channels reversing at −65 mV, transduction cation channels reversing near 0 mV), why is the receptor potential graded?
cards.back: A stronger stimulus opens more transduction channels, and each one pulls the conductance-weighted balance point further toward 0 mV, so the voltage moves further.
cards.quote: Each extra open transduction channel pulls the balance point toward 0 mV.
cards.section: Why the receptor potential is graded

cards.front: In a passive receptor model, the resting conductance is 1 (reversal −65 mV) and the transduction conductance reverses at 0 mV (made-up units). What is the balance point when the transduction conductance is 4, and when it is 9? What does the comparison show?
cards.back: V = (1 × −65 + g × 0) ÷ (1 + g). At g = 4: −65 ÷ 5 = −13 mV. At g = 9: −65 ÷ 10 = −6.5 mV. Five more units move it only 6.5 mV: the response saturates.
cards.why: The voltage can approach the transduction reversal of 0 mV but never pass it (the driving-force limit).
cards.quote: Each equal increase moves it less, by about 11, 5 and 3 mV, because the voltage can approach 0 mV but never pass it.
cards.section: Why the receptor potential is graded

cards.front: Why does light hyperpolarize a vertebrate rod?
cards.back: cGMP-gated cation channels are open in the dark, and light closes them. Losing that cation conductance moves the balance point away from 0 mV, so the inside becomes more negative.
cards.quote: In a rod, cGMP-gated cation channels are open in the dark, and light closes them.
cards.section: Why the receptor potential is graded

cards.front: Why must a receptor potential be turned into spikes to reach the spinal cord or brain?
cards.back: It spreads passively and fades over about a length constant. Spikes regenerate along the way.
cards.quote: A passive potential fades as it spreads, over about a length constant.

cards.front: Contrast how the receptor potential drives the afferent when the ending is part of the afferent neuron and when the receptor is a separate cell.
cards.back: Part of the afferent (most touch): it depolarizes the spike-initiating zone, and the larger it is, the faster the firing. Separate cell (taste cells, photoreceptors): it changes transmitter release onto the next cell.
cards.quote: The receptor potential depolarizes the spike-initiating zone, where the axon's spikes start, and the larger it is, the faster the neuron fires action potentials.

cards.front: A {{c1::receptive field}} is the region of the sensory surface, a patch of skin or of the visual field, where a stimulus can change a given cell's activity.
cards.quote: A receptive field is the region of the sensory surface, a patch of skin or of the visual field, where a stimulus can change a given cell's activity.
cards.section: Where and when: receptive fields and adaptation

cards.front: A skin region has few afferents per square millimetre, and their receptive fields are large and overlapping. Predict how well it resolves two blunt points touched a short distance apart, and why.
cards.back: Poorly. Two nearby points tend to fall in the same afferents' fields and drive the same lines, so the spatial picture is coarse, as on the back rather than the fingertip.
cards.quote: On the back, afferents are sparser and their fields larger and overlapping, so the spatial picture is coarser and two nearby points are harder to resolve.
cards.section: Where and when: receptive fields and adaptation

cards.front: Contrast rapidly and slowly adapting skin endings during a maintained stimulus.
cards.back: Rapidly adapting endings fire at the start, then fall quiet (many fire again at removal): they signal change. Slowly adapting endings fire for as long as the stimulus lasts: they report the stimulus itself.
cards.quote: Rapidly adapting endings fire at the start of a maintained stimulus and then fall quiet; many fire again when it is removed.
cards.section: Where and when: receptive fields and adaptation

cards.front: A probe indents the skin steadily while a vibration is added on top. Which class of touch afferent reports each component, and why?
cards.back: Slowly adapting afferents (such as Merkel-cell afferents) report the steady indentation. Rapidly adapting afferents (such as Pacinian afferents) report the vibration.
cards.why: Adaptation is tuning in time: rapidly adapting endings are tuned to change, slowly adapting endings report the stimulus itself.
cards.quote: They are tuned to change: a Pacinian corpuscle in the skin signals vibration.
cards.section: Where and when: receptive fields and adaptation

cards.front: In the Limulus lateral eye, lighting an ommatidium's neighbours reduced its discharge. How did Hartline and colleagues rule out stray light or optics?
cards.back: They cut the lateral connections to the recorded ommatidium, and the neighbours' light no longer inhibited it. The inhibition ran through connections among the units.
cards.quote: So they cut the lateral connections to the recorded ommatidium, and the neighbours' light no longer inhibited it.

cards.front: Six receptors in a row receive excitation 10, 10, 10, 30, 30, 30 (made-up units), and the row continues beyond both ends. Each output = own excitation − 0.2 × (left neighbour + right neighbour). Give the outputs of the dim interior, dim edge, bright edge and bright interior units.
cards.back: Dim interior: 10 − 0.2 × 20 = 6. Dim edge: 10 − 0.2 × 40 = 2. Bright edge: 30 − 0.2 × 40 = 22. Bright interior: 30 − 0.2 × 60 = 18. The dim edge dips below its plateau and the bright edge rises above its own.
cards.quote: output = own excitation − 0.2 × (left neighbour + right neighbour)

cards.front: In the feedforward lateral-inhibition model of a row of receptors, what happens to the step at an edge and to the uniform regions on either side?
cards.back: The step across the edge keeps its size, while the difference between the plateaus shrinks. Uniform regions are discounted, so the edge stands out against them.
cards.quote: So lateral inhibition discounts uniform regions, and the edge stands out against them.

cards.front: Using contrast = (bright − dim) ÷ (bright + dim): a row with input 10 and 30 gives lateral-inhibition outputs of 6 and 18 on the plateaus and 2 and 22 at the edge. Compute the contrast of the input, of the output plateaus, and across the edge.
cards.back: Input: 20 ÷ 40 = 0.5. Output plateaus: 12 ÷ 24 = 0.5. Across the edge: 20 ÷ 24 ≈ 0.83. The edge keeps its step while the levels around it fall, so its contrast rises.
cards.quote: Contrast, (bright − dim) ÷ (bright + dim), puts a number on standing out

cards.front: d′ = change in mean rate ÷ {{c1::noise}}, where the noise is the trial-to-trial standard deviation of the spike count.
cards.quote: What matters is the gap between the two means in units of noise, called d′
cards.section: From a tuning curve to a threshold

cards.front: With equal noise at every stimulus, why is fine discrimination often best on a tuning curve's steep flank rather than at its peak?
cards.back: For a small change, d′ ≈ slope × change ÷ noise. At the peak the slope is near zero, so a small change barely moves the mean rate; on the flank it moves it a lot.
cards.quote: The peak is where a neuron fires most, not where it discriminates best.
cards.section: From a tuning curve to a threshold

cards.front: A neuron fires 80, 70, 30 and 10 spikes/s at 0, 10, 20 and 30 degrees, changing in a straight line between those angles, with noise of 4 spikes/s at every angle (made-up). Compare d′ for a 2-degree change within the 0–10 segment and within the 10–20 segment.
cards.back: Slopes: 10 ÷ 10 = 1 and 40 ÷ 10 = 4 spikes/s per degree. Peak segment: d′ = (1 × 2) ÷ 4 = 0.5. Flank segment: d′ = (4 × 2) ÷ 4 = 2.0, four times larger, so the flank change is easier to detect.
cards.quote: d′ ≈ (slope of the tuning curve × change in stimulus) ÷ noise
cards.section: From a tuning curve to a threshold

cards.front: Real spike counts are noisier at higher rates, with variance roughly tracking the mean. How does this change the comparison between a tuning curve's peak and its flank for fine discrimination?
cards.back: It favours the flank even more. The high-rate peak has the larger noise, which lowers its d′ further.
cards.quote: Real spike counts are noisier when the rate is higher, with the variance roughly tracking the mean, and that counts against the high-rate peak even more.
cards.section: From a tuning curve to a threshold

cards.front: In a fixed fine-discrimination comparison between a tuning curve's flank and its peak, the same noise is doubled at every stimulus. Does the flank still win, and roughly what happens to the thresholds?
cards.back: The flank still wins. Doubling the noise everywhere halves every d′ for a fixed stimulus pair, so the ranking holds. Thresholds roughly double only where the tuning curve is locally linear with a nonzero slope.
cards.why: d′ = change in mean rate ÷ noise; the same factor on every noise scales every d′ equally.
cards.quote: raising the same noise everywhere scales every d′ equally
cards.section: When noise moves the best stimulus

cards.front: Assume an afferent's mean firing rate saturates with stimulus strength, so its rate-versus-strength slope is smallest at high strengths, and the noise is equal at all strengths. Predict where small changes in strength are hardest to detect from its firing.
cards.back: At high strengths. There the slope is smallest, so a fixed small change moves the mean rate least and d′ is smallest.
cards.why: Rests on the stated rule that a small change is easiest to detect where it moves the mean rate a lot compared with the noise; the saturating rate is the assumption.
cards.quote: for otherwise similar responses, a small change is easiest to detect where it moves the mean rate a lot compared with the noise

cards.front: A {{c1::psychometric function}} plots an observer's performance against the size of the stimulus difference.
cards.quote: A psychometric function plots an observer's performance against the size of the stimulus difference

cards.front: In a two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) task, what score is chance, and where does a common convention set the threshold?
cards.back: 50% correct is chance, since a guess is right half the time. A common threshold is 75% correct, halfway between chance and perfect.
cards.quote: A common convention puts the threshold halfway between chance and perfect, at 75% correct

cards.front: Assume an ideal observer compares one neuron's spike counts from two intervals, with independent, equally noisy Gaussian counts. Then proportion correct = Φ(d′ ÷ √2). Why the √2?
cards.back: Independent variances add, σ² + σ² = 2σ², so the difference of the two counts has standard deviation √2σ, which is √2 times as noisy as either one.
cards.quote: their difference is √2 times as noisy as either one

cards.front: For an ideal 2AFC observer reading one neuron, assuming independent Gaussian spike counts with equal noise for both stimuli, what d′ gives 75% correct, and what does that make the neuron's threshold?
cards.back: A d′ of about 0.95. So the neuron's threshold is roughly the stimulus change that moves its mean rate by one noise unit.
cards.quote: So a neuron's threshold is roughly the stimulus change that moves its mean rate by one noise unit.

cards.front: A neuron's tuning curve has a slope of 4 spikes/s per degree on its flank and 1 spike/s per degree near its peak, with noise of 4 spikes/s everywhere. Taking threshold as d′ ≈ 0.95 (75% correct in 2AFC), estimate its threshold at each place.
cards.back: Change = d′ × noise ÷ slope. Flank: 0.95 × 4 ÷ 4 ≈ 0.95 degrees. Peak: 0.95 × 4 ÷ 1 ≈ 3.8 degrees, four times coarser.
cards.quote: Reaching 75% correct takes a d′ of about 0.95.

cards.front: A model 2AFC observer follows p(x) = 0.5 + 0.5 × Φ((x − 3°) / 1.5°), where Φ is the standard normal cumulative distribution and Φ(0.84) = 0.80. What is the 75% threshold, and what difference x gives 90% correct?
cards.quote: Step 2: 90% correct. Φ(z) = (0.90 − 0.5)/0.5 = 0.8, so z = 0.84 and x = 2.84 degrees.
cards.section: Reading a psychometric function in numbers

cards.front: Monkeys reported which of two opposite directions a field of dots drifted, at varying motion coherence, while single MT neurons were recorded with the display matched to each neuron's receptive field and preferred direction. What was compared, and what was found?
cards.back: Each neuron's neurometric function, built from its spike counts on the same trials, against the monkey's psychometric function. Most neurons were about as sensitive as the monkey.
cards.quote: Under these conditions, most neurons were about as sensitive as the monkey.

cards.front: A single MT neuron is about as sensitive to motion direction as the monkey performing the task. Does this show that the neuron made the monkey's choice?
cards.back: No. It shows that one neuron's spike count holds about as much signal as the monkey used: a statement about signal, not cause. Many MT neurons respond to the same dots.
cards.quote: One neuron's spike count holds about as much signal as the monkey used: a statement about signal, not cause.

cards.front: Many MT neurons are each about as sensitive as the monkey. If their noise were independent, what would pooling them predict for the monkey's sensitivity, and why does the prediction fail?
cards.back: Averaging would make the monkey far more sensitive than any one neuron, and it is not. In a model by the same group, neighbouring neurons' noise is weakly correlated, and shared noise cannot be averaged away.
cards.why: In that model, pools of at least 100 weakly correlated neurons fit best: a model estimate, not a count.
cards.quote: Noise they share rises and falls together, so averaging cannot cancel it.

cards.front: To go from "MT neurons carry enough signal to match behaviour" to "MT activity contributes to the motion judgement", what kind of experiment is needed, and what result supported it?
cards.back: A manipulation of MT activity during the task. Microstimulating MT biased the monkeys' choices (Salzman, Britten and Newsome, 1990).
cards.why: Matching sensitivity is a statement about signal; cause needs an intervention.
cards.quote: Whether MT activity causes the judgement takes a manipulation.

cards.front: In a population code for stimulus quality, how is the quality read?
cards.back: From the pattern of rates across many fibres, rather than from which single dedicated line is active.
cards.quote: Quality can be carried by a labelled line or by a population code, read from the pattern of rates across many fibres.
cards.section: Lines or patterns: coding what kind of stimulus

cards.front: In mice, sweet taste cells were made to express a receptor for a synthetic opiate, and the mice became attracted to that drug. What coding scheme does this support, and at what level?
cards.back: Dedicated (labelled) lines at the level of taste cells: activating sweet cells produces attraction whatever the ligand.
cards.quote: making sweet cells express a receptor for a synthetic opiate made mice attracted to that drug
cards.section: Lines or patterns: coding what kind of stimulus

cards.front: How is odorant identity coded at the level of olfactory receptors?
cards.back: By a combination: one receptor recognizes several odorants, and one odorant is recognized by several receptors. Smell leans toward population coding.
cards.quote: one receptor recognizes several odorants and one odorant is recognized by several receptors, so an odorant is coded by a combination
cards.section: Lines or patterns: coding what kind of stimulus

cards.front: In mouse geniculate taste neurons, 28 of 101 responded to more than one taste below the EC50, and 79 of 155 did so at about 1.5 to 2 times the EC50. A classmate says this refutes labelled lines. Evaluate the claim.
cards.back: 28% rises to 51%, but the samples differ, so stronger evidence is the same neuron at two concentrations. Broad peripheral tuning says what the ganglion sends, not how the brain decodes it. It is a scoped counterexample, not a refutation.
cards.quote: The result is a scoped counterexample to strict, concentration-invariant labelled lines in mouse geniculate neurons, not a refutation of every labelled-line model.

cards.front: To test whether a dedicated "sweet" line carries taste quality, you silence one molecularly defined group of afferents. Why is a loss of sweet responses alone not decisive, and what measure would separate the models?
cards.back: A pattern decoder could also lose sweet when its main input is gone. Measure discrimination among the remaining tastes at low and high concentrations: a pattern code using those fibres should blur it, most where tuning is broad.
cards.quote: A pattern decoder could also lose sweet when its main input is gone, so a loss of sweet alone does not separate the models.

cards.front: What class of receptor protein transduces smell and sweet, umami and bitter taste, and what transduces sour taste?
cards.back: G-protein-coupled receptors for smell and for sweet, umami and bitter. Sour taste works through the proton channel OTOP1.
cards.quote: The receptor proteins for smell and for sweet, umami and bitter taste are G-protein-coupled receptors.
